title: REDs: what low energy costs
goal: Explain how low energy availability changes hormones, periods, bone, metabolism, mood and performance, how the female athlete triad grew into REDs, and what it means for male athletes and cyclists.

steps.title: From the triad to REDs
steps.text:
In its 2007 position stand, the American College of Sports Medicine defined the [female athlete triad](g:female-athlete-triad): energy availability, menstrual function and bone density, linked on a spectrum from healthy to ill. At the ill end sit eating disorders, [amenorrhoea](g:amenorrhoea) and osteoporosis [[c:rc-triad-def]].

In 2014 the IOC widened it to RED-S. Two changes: men are affected too, and the harm reaches far beyond three systems, to metabolic rate, immunity, protein synthesis, heart and blood vessels, and mental health, which can be a cause or a result [[c:rc-reds-2014]].

The 2023 update (written [REDs](g:reds)) kept that wide view and added more on mental health and on men [[c:rc-reds-2023]].

claims.text: The female athlete triad describes interrelated energy availability, menstrual function and bone mineral density, with eating disorders, functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea and osteoporosis at the clinical end.

evidence.quote: The female athlete triad (Triad) refers to the interrelationships among energy availability, menstrual function, and bone mineral density, which may have clinical manifestations including eating disorders, functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, and osteoporosis.

claims.text: RED-S (IOC 2014) affects men too and many functions, including metabolic rate, menstrual function, bone, immunity, protein synthesis and cardiovascular health; psychological problems can precede or follow it.

evidence.quote: The term 'Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport' (RED-S), points to the complexity involved and the fact that male athletes are also affected.

The syndrome of RED-S refers to impaired physiological function including, but not limited to, metabolic rate, menstrual function, bone health, immunity, protein synthesis, cardiovascular health caused by relative energy deficiency.
Psychological consequences can either precede RED-S or be the result of RED-S.

claims.text: The 2023 IOC update adds evidence on mental health and on low energy availability in males.

evidence.quote: Since the 2018 REDs consensus, there have been >170 original research publications advancing the field of REDs science, including emerging data demonstrating the growing role of low carbohydrate availability, further evidence of the interplay between mental health and REDs and more data elucidating the impact of LEA in males.

steps.title: The body's energy-saving mode
steps.text:
When energy runs short, the body turns down what it can do without. Lab studies show the pattern:

- [T3](g:triiodothyronine), the active thyroid hormone, falls (consistently in women), so resting energy use drops [[c:rc-t3]].
- [Leptin](g:leptin), insulin and [IGF-1](g:igf-1) fall; IGF-1 drops when EA goes below about 84 kJ (20 kcal). [Cortisol](g:cortisol) tends to rise [[c:rc-igf]].
- LH pulses slow, so the ovaries make less [oestrogen](g:oestrogen). Over time, periods can stop: [functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea](g:functional-hypothalamic-amenorrhoea), which is reversible [[c:rc-fha]].

Each change saves energy. Together they explain why one deficit shows up in bone, muscle, blood and mood.

claims.text: T3 is consistently reduced by low energy availability, at least in females.

evidence.quote: The majority of subsequent studies have reported that T 3 , the active form of the hormone, is consistently reduced in response to LEA at least in females (Table 3 ), while changes in T 4 -its precursor- are ambiguous (Loucks and Callister 1993 ; Loucks and Heath 1994a ).

claims.text: Low EA lowers IGF-1 below about 20 kcal·kg LBM⁻¹·day⁻¹, lowers leptin and insulin, and tends to raise cortisol; it suppresses oestrogen, testosterone, leptin, T3 and IGF-1.

evidence.quote: Similarly, LEA consistently increases circulating GH with a concomitant reduction of circulating IGF-1 when EA < 20 kcal/kg LBM/day (Table 2 ).

Cortisol has not been reported consistently in the LEA literature, but measured as 24 h transverse mean it has been shown to increase with EA ≤ 30 kcal/kg LBM/day in studies incorporating exercise to achieve LEA.

LEA is characterized by the perturbation of several hormones involved in the regulation of bone (re)modelling, including the suppression of estrogen, testosterone, leptin, triiodothyronine, and insulin-like growth factor 1, and an increase in adiponectin [ 6 – 10 ].
Following both low energy availability conditions, leptin (-53% to -56%) and insulin (-34% to -38%) were reduced (P < 0.05).

claims.text: Low energy availability causes menstrual disturbances, the most severe being functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea, a reversible state with chronic oestrogen deficiency.

evidence.quote: LEA also causes menstrual disturbances [ 17 ], the most severe being functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA), a reversible cause of ovarian disruption characterized by the absence of menses and chronic estrogen deficiency [ 4 ].

steps.title: Bone takes two hits
steps.text:
You saw in the body composition module that [bone stress injuries](g:bone-stress-injury) were about 4.5 times more common in amenorrhoeic women and low-[testosterone](g:testosterone) men. Here is why.

Bone loses twice. Low energy cuts bone-building directly (the 5-day lab study), and the low oestrogen that follows also weakens bone. The two add up [[c:rc-bone-additive]]. Female runners with low EA have lower [BMD](g:bone-mineral-density) and thinner, narrower bones, and those with FHA have more bone stress injuries [[c:rc-bone-runners]].

One possible help is short, high-impact jumping: it builds bone at little energy cost. Evidence during low EA is still early [[c:rc-jumps]]. Bone injury itself belongs to the injury module.

claims.text: Energy deficiency and oestrogen deficiency have additive harmful effects on bone.

evidence.quote: Interactions between energy and estrogen deficiency lead to additive decrements to bone [ 53 ], yet both may exert independent effects also [ 46 ].

claims.text: Female weight-bearing endurance athletes with low EA show lower BMD, smaller and thinner bones; those with FHA have more bone stress injuries.

evidence.quote: Female weight-bearing endurance athletes with symptoms of low energy availability exhibit lower bone mineral density, total and cross-sectional area, estimated strength and thinner cortices, each of which may contribute to the development of bone stress injury.
Female athletes with FHA suffer more bone stress injuries, and more miss training days due to injury, compared to their eumenorrheic counterparts [ 5 , 21 , 22 ].

claims.text: High-impact exercise is osteogenic at low energy cost and may help counter low EA effects on bone, but evidence during LEA is preliminary.

evidence.quote: High-impact exercise may offer a time and energy efficient solution to counter the effects of low energy availability on bone in situations where restoration of energy availability is difficult.

There is evidence to suggest that a high-impact intervention may help mitigate the effects of LEA on bone strength; however, further research needs to be conducted before it could be considered a viable tool to protect athletes suffering LEA from bone stress injury.

steps.title: Slower, not just less healthy
steps.text:
Health effects matter on their own, but low energy also costs performance.

Ten junior elite swimmers were followed for a 12-week season. Those whose ovarian hormones were suppressed also had lower T3, IGF-1 and energy availability. Their 400 m speed fell by 9.8%; the swimmers with normal cycles improved by 8.2% [[c:rc-swim]].

In a 14-day study, 12 male endurance athletes had their energy availability cut by a quarter, to about 94 kJ (22 kcal). Explosive power and [haemoglobin](g:haemoglobin) fell and well-being got worse, before any hormone change showed [[c:rc-jurov]].

Both studies are small, and the swimmers weren't randomised. But they point the same way as larger surveys: a weaker training response and poorer endurance.

claims.text: Ovarian-suppressed junior elite swimmers with low T3 and IGF-1 slowed 400 m swim velocity by 9.8% over 12 weeks while cyclic swimmers improved by 8.2%.

evidence.quote: OVS exhibited a 9.8% decline in Δ400-m swim velocity compared with an 8.2% improvement in CYC at week 12.

Total triiodothyronine (TT3) and insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) were lower in OVS (TT3: CYC = 1.6 ± 0.2 nmol·L, OVS = 1.4 ± 0.1 nmol·L, P < 0.001; IGF-1: CYC = 243 ± 1 μg·mL, OVS = 214 ± 3 μg·mL P < 0.001) than CYC at week 12.

claims.text: In 12 male endurance athletes, 14 days of EA reduced by 25% (to about 22 kcal·kg FFM⁻¹·day⁻¹) lowered explosive power and haemoglobin and worsened well-being before hormonal changes.

evidence.quote: Reduced energy availability (22.4 ± 6.3 kcal/kg FFM/day) caused significantly lower haemoglobin values (t(12) = 2.652, p = 0.022), there was a tendency for lower iron and IGF-1 (p = 0.066 and p = 0.077, respectively).
This is the first research providing direct evidence that suboptimal energy availability negatively impacts explosive power before hormonal changes occur in male endurance athletes.

steps.title: Men and cyclists
steps.text:
Men seem to need a deeper or longer deficit before hormones change, but the data are thin [[c:rc-male-less]].

Road cyclists are a group to watch. Among 50 competitive male road cyclists, 28% had low energy availability and 44% had a low lumbar spine BMD ([Z-score](g:z-score) below −1). Energy availability was the strongest predictor of spine BMD; those who had never done a load-bearing sport had the lowest. Cyclists with long-term low EA had lower testosterone [[c:rc-keay]].

Mood and health suffer in men too. In male athletes at sports clinics, signs of low EA went with about 3 times the [odds](g:odds-ratio) of psychological illness and more reports of poorer training response and endurance [[c:rc-holtzman]].

claims.text: Early findings suggest men may be less sensitive to reduced energy availability, but research in males is limited.

evidence.quote: Although current research on males is limited, early findings suggest that men may be less sensitive to reductions in energy availability.

claims.text: In 50 male road cyclists, 28% had low EA and 44% low lumbar BMD (Z < −1); EA was the strongest determinant of spine BMD; chronic low EA was linked to lower testosterone.

evidence.quote: Low EA as assessed using the SEAQ-I, was observed in 28% of cyclists.
Low lumbar spine BMD (Z-score<-1.0) was found in 44% of cyclists.
EA was the most significant determinant of lumbar spine BMD Z-score (p<0.001).
The 10 cyclists with chronic low EA had lower levels of testosterone compared with those having adequate EA (p=0.024).

claims.text: In male athletes, low EA surrogates were associated with psychological illness (OR 3.23), decreased training response and endurance performance.

evidence.quote: Low EA athletes were more likely to have self-reported cardiovascular dysfunction (OR 2.87, 95% CI 1.56 to 5.26) and psychological illness (OR 3.23, 95% CI 1.91 to 5.41), decreased training response (OR 2.64, 95% CI 1.38 to 5.03) and endurance performance (OR 2.26, 95% CI 1.13 to 4.52) and were less likely to have self-reported gonadal dysfunction (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.81), than adequate EA athletes (p<0.05).

points: The female athlete triad (energy, periods, bone) became RED-S (2014) and REDs (2023): men too, and many systems, including immunity and mental health.
Low energy turns the body to saving mode: T3, leptin, insulin and IGF-1 fall, cortisol rises, LH pulses slow and oestrogen or testosterone drop.
Bone takes two hits, low energy and low sex hormones; women with FHA get more bone stress injuries. Impact jumps may help, early evidence.
Performance suffers too: small studies show slower swimmers and lower power in men within two weeks.
Men seem to need a deeper deficit, but road cyclists often show low EA, low spine BMD and lower testosterone.

variants.stem: What did the IOC's RED-S model (2014) add to the female athlete triad?

options.text: It includes men and many more body systems, such as immunity and metabolism
options.why: Right: RED-S is a wider syndrome, not a triad of three conditions in women.

options.text: It replaced energy availability with body fat as the cause
options.why: Low energy availability stays the cause in both models.

options.text: It limited the problem to elite athletes only
options.why: Both models apply to anyone who trains; neither is limited to elites.

options.text: It dropped bone health from the model
options.why: Bone health stays central in REDs.

variants.stem: A male cyclist asks whether the "female athlete triad" applies to him. What is the best answer?

options.text: The triad was for women; REDs includes men and covers more systems
options.why: Right: the 2014 IOC model was renamed partly because men are affected too.

options.text: No: low energy availability only harms women
options.why: Men are affected too, though they may need a deeper deficit.

options.text: Yes: the triad was always defined for both sexes
options.why: The triad was defined in active women; REDs extended it to men.

options.text: Only if he has stopped growing taller
options.why: Age and growth aren't the point; energy availability is.

variants.stem: A runner's blood test shows low T3, low IGF-1, low oestrogen and a cortisol at the top of normal. Her thyroid gland itself is healthy. What is the most likely common thread?

options.text: The body saving energy because energy availability is low
options.why: Right: all four fit the energy-saving pattern of low EA.

options.text: Overactive thyroid speeding up her metabolism
options.why: Low T3 means a slower, not faster, resting metabolism.

options.text: Too much carbohydrate raising her hormones
options.why: These hormones are mostly lowered, not raised, and carbohydrate excess doesn't explain it.

options.text: Normal training adaptation that needs no follow-up
options.why: Training alone with enough energy doesn't push these hormones down together.

variants.stem: A male triathlete has low T3, low IGF-1 and low testosterone, with no disease of the thyroid or testes found. What best explains the pattern?

options.text: Low energy availability turning down energy-costly systems
options.why: Right: the hormones fall together as the body saves energy.

options.text: A genetic hormone disorder present since birth
options.why: Low values found together after hard training point first to energy, not a birth disorder.

options.text: Too much protein in his diet
options.why: Protein intake doesn't lower these three together.

options.text: Normal adaptation: fitter athletes always have lower hormones
options.why: Training adaptation doesn't explain this combined fall.

variants.stem: Why does a fall in T3 make sense when energy availability is low?

options.text: Lower T3 slows resting energy use, saving energy
options.why: Right: T3 sets the resting burn rate, so lower T3 spends less.

options.text: Lower T3 speeds up fat burning to cover the gap
options.why: T3 falling slows metabolism overall; it doesn't speed it up.

options.text: Lower T3 raises appetite so intake catches up
options.why: That isn't T3's main role, and appetite often doesn't rise enough.

options.text: Lower T3 makes muscles contract more efficiently in races
options.why: There is no such performance benefit; it is a saving response.

variants.stem: Why is bone hit especially hard in a woman with low energy availability and missing periods?

options.text: Low energy cuts bone-building, and low oestrogen weakens bone too
options.why: Right: the energy and oestrogen deficits add up.

options.text: Missing periods mean she loses calcium in menstrual blood
options.why: She is losing no blood; the point is oestrogen's role in bone.

options.text: Low energy makes bone grow too fast and become brittle
options.why: Bone-building slows, it doesn't speed up.

options.text: Only her body fat matters; hormones don't affect bone
options.why: Oestrogen is a key protector of bone.

variants.stem: A road cyclist with low BMD is restoring her energy intake, which will take months. What added step fits the evidence best, with its limits?

options.text: Short, high-impact jumps a few times a week; promising, but early evidence
options.why: Right: impact builds bone at little energy cost; data during low EA are preliminary.

options.text: More long rides, since cycling loads bone strongly
options.why: Cycling gives bone little impact; more riding also raises energy needs.

options.text: Long slow swims, since water training loads bone
options.why: Swimming is non-impact and does little for bone.

options.text: Nothing: bone can't respond to exercise in adults
options.why: Adult bone does respond to high-impact loading.

variants.stem: A male triathlete, mostly cycling and swimming, has low BMD after a lean season. Besides eating more, which training change has the best rationale?

options.text: Add brief, high-impact jumping, which loads bone at little energy cost
options.why: Right: impact loading builds bone cheaply, though evidence during low EA is early.

options.text: Drop all running to protect his bones
options.why: Running gives bone the impact it needs; removing it removes the stimulus.

options.text: Swim more, as water pressure loads the skeleton
options.why: Swimming gives little bone loading.

options.text: Add long low-power rides for more volume
options.why: Cycling gives bone little load and costs more energy.

variants.stem: The swimmer study found a 9.8% slowdown in ovarian-suppressed swimmers versus an 8.2% gain in the others. What most limits the conclusion that low energy caused the slowdown?

options.text: Only 10 swimmers, and groups formed by hormone status, not at random
options.why: Right: tiny and observational, so other differences between groups could explain it.

options.text: Swimming speed can't be measured reliably over 400 m
options.why: Timed 400 m swims are a standard, reliable test.

options.text: 12 weeks is too long to see any change
options.why: 12 weeks is long enough; the problem is the design and size.

options.text: The effect is too large to be real, so it must be an error
options.why: A large effect in a small study is a reason for caution, not proof of error; the design is the main limit.

variants.stem: A coach cites the 10-swimmer study as proof that restoring periods makes any athlete 18% faster. What is the main problem?

options.text: A small observational study can't show cause, or a size for everyone
options.why: Right: groups weren't randomised, and 10 junior swimmers can't set an effect for all athletes.

options.text: Swimmers' results never apply to land sports
options.why: Physiology often transfers; the problem is design and size.

options.text: The study found no difference between the groups
options.why: It found a clear difference; the issue is what it can prove.

options.text: It measured men, so it can't apply to women
options.why: All 10 swimmers were female.

variants.stem: A male cyclist cuts his energy availability by a quarter for two weeks before a stage race to lose weight. Based on the 14-day study in male endurance athletes, which change is he most likely to notice first?

options.text: Poorer sprint power and lower well-being, before hormones change
options.why: Right: explosive power and well-being fell, haemoglobin dropped, before hormone changes showed.

options.text: Lower testosterone, with power unchanged
options.why: Testosterone didn't change in that time; power did.

options.text: Higher power-to-weight with no downside
options.why: Power fell and well-being worsened.

options.text: Stopped bone growth within days, with no other effect
options.why: Bone wasn't the measured outcome; power and haemoglobin were.

variants.stem: Two male road cyclists both have low energy availability. One ran cross-country at school; the other has only ever cycled. Who most likely has the lower spine BMD, and why?

options.text: The pure cyclist: no history of impact loading on top of low EA
options.why: Right: among low-EA cyclists, no past load-bearing sport went with the lowest BMD.

options.text: The ex-runner: running wears bone down
options.why: Impact loading builds bone; it is the lack of it that hurts.

options.text: Neither: cycling builds bone as much as running
options.why: Cycling gives bone little impact load.

options.text: Both the same: only current energy matters
options.why: Past loading made a difference among low-EA cyclists.

variants.stem: In a group of 50 male road cyclists, which factor predicted lumbar spine BMD most strongly?

options.text: Energy availability
options.why: Right: EA was the most significant determinant of spine BMD Z-score.

options.text: Body fat percentage
options.why: Body fat wasn't the main predictor; EA was.

options.text: Training hours per week
options.why: Training hours weren't the main predictor; EA was.

options.text: Bike weight
options.why: Equipment wasn't a factor; energy was.

variants.stem: What does current research suggest about men compared with women at the same low energy availability?

options.text: Men may need a deeper or longer deficit before hormones change; data are thin
options.why: Right: early findings suggest men are less sensitive, but research is limited.

options.text: Men are fully protected and can't develop REDs
options.why: Men do develop REDs: low testosterone, low BMD and mood effects.

options.text: Men are more sensitive and react at higher EA than women
options.why: Early data suggest the opposite.

options.text: Men and women respond identically at every level
options.why: Responses seem to differ by sex.
